Introduction:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the leading cause of respiratory mortality globally, leading to over 3 million deaths per year. 1 Smoking is considered the primary cause of COPD and, historically, has been largely focused on as part of the control of COPD. 2 However, there is a growing realization that a large proportion of COPD cannot be explained by smoking, and that there may be important secondary risk factors. 3

There is mounting concern about the possible impact of pulmonary tuberculosis on long-term lung health. 4–7 Several studies have reported persistence of airway obstruction as well as chronic or recurrent symptoms after individuals recover from tuberculosis. 6 , 8 Tuberculosis may result in significant lung impairment; however, whether residual lung damage due to tuberculosis results in clinically significant outcomes has not been well studied. Although tuberculosis has been mentioned in some COPD guidelines, there is limited evidence of an association. 2 Few studies have assessed the relationship between prior tuberculosis and the subsequent development of COPD. Most of these studies have assessed tuberculosis diagnoses retrospectively or through self-report, and have been located in settings with a low burden of COPD, limiting generalizability. 9–14 Furthermore, whether an association between tuberculosis and subsequent development of COPD is independent of smoking status, a risk factor for both diseases, is not well elucidated. 2

China is going through large-scale health transitions. 15 , 16 An estimated 100 million people in China are estimated to have COPD, accounting for approximately 25% of total cases worldwide. 17 , 18 Tobacco use and an aging population are considered leading risk factors for this increasing COPD burden; however, risk factors for COPD beyond these, in China and more broadly, are not well understood. 2 , 3 , 13

To attempt to improve our understanding of the risk of COPD after developing tuberculosis, we used the Chinese Electronic Health Records Research in Yinzhou (CHERRY) study, a large, ambispective, population-based, observational cohort of participants in a setting with a high burden of COPD. 19 We assessed the association between tuberculosis and the subsequent development of COPD, adjusted for a range of potential confounders. We then evaluated whether important secondary characteristics, such as smoking status, modified this relationship.
Methods:
### Study design and data source

We performed a longitudinal cohort study using the CHERRY, a population-based electronic health database established in 2006 and containing 98% of permanent adult residents in Yinzhou ( Supplementary Figure S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). 19 This database has been used extensively in our previous epidemiological studies. 20–22 The CHERRY is based on the Yinzhou Health Information System (YHIS) that contains comprehensive information, such as health check information, inpatient and outpatient electronic medical records, chronic disease surveillance system and death certificates. These databases are inherently linked to each other by a unique and encoded individual identifier. 19 In Yinzhou district in Ningbo, 96% of permanent residents are covered by the health insurance system. Residents of all ages are covered by the system; however only adults above 18 years of age on 1 January 2009 are included in the CHERRY Study. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Zhejiang University School of Public Health.

### Identification of study cohort

In order to bypass the integration and preliminary test period of the system and to allow for full coverage of the regional population, we recruited residents who had registered in the CHERRY during 1 January 2009 to 31 December 2014. Exclusion criteria included age <35 years, participants with a previous history of COPD or with a previous history of cancer and participants with missing values of covariates. We excluded younger participants because the vast majority of COPD occurs >35 years of age. The cohort was dynamic and therefore participants could enter at different time points if they had the exposure at baseline or during follow-up.

### Identification of tuberculosis and COPD

The exposure of interest was tuberculosis, from the health insurance database. In China, tuberculosis care is provided by the national government special funds and has a wide and comprehensive coverage rate. Tuberculosis events were recorded based on the Chinese National Disease Reporting system which includes all diagnosed tuberculosis cases at the city, provincial and national levels. 23–26 The definition of pulmonary tuberculosis disease and all tuberculosis was based on the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) codes ( Supplementary Table S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). Due to the dynamic nature of the cohort, persons could contribute to the unexposed and, if they were diagnosed with tuberculosis during follow-up, also to the exposed ( Supplementary Table S2 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online).

We identified participants with the outcome as those diagnosed with COPD, defined by ICD-10 codes ( Supplementary Table S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online) during the study period (1 January 2009 to 30 September 2021). 27 The diagnostic date of COPD was defined as the endpoint date for persons developing COPD.

### Measurement of covariates

Demographic characteristics were collected as part of the baseline survey and included lifestyle factors, socioeconomic status, comorbidities and use of medications. Demographic characteristics included age, sex and marital status. Lifestyle factors were recorded at baseline, including smoking intensity, alcohol consumption, physical activity and body mass index (BMI). We dichotomized weight into a group that was either overweight or obese (≥24 kg/m 2 and over) or normal and underweight (<24 kg/m 2 ). 28 , 29 Smoking intensity was defined as the average number of cigarettes smoked per day. Current alcohol drinking was defined as drinking at least 100 grams of any alcohol per week during the past year. Education level was measured at the baseline visit and included illiterate, primary school, middle school and high school and above. Important factors related to COPD were also considered, including diabetes, hypertension, asthma, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, arrhythmia, ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke, heart failure, depression, anxiety, osteoporosis and the use of COPD medications ( Supplementary Tables S1 and S3 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online).

### Statistical analysis

We used Cox proportional hazards survival time regression models to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations of tuberculosis or pulmonary tuberculosis with risk of subsequent COPD. For COPD incidence, time-to-event data were constructed at first date of study recruitment and/or the date of tuberculosis diagnosis. Participants could have entered the study as unexposed (no history of tuberculosis) and then become exposed over follow-up upon developing tuberculosis. In the analysis, once COPD occurs, participants could no longer contribute to follow-up, regardless of their exposure status. We excluded 126 new cases of tuberculosis after a COPD diagnosis. Follow-up was censored at death or end of follow-up. The time to event in exposed and unexposed groups was defined as the time interval between the date participants were registered in the YHIS (or the time of TB diagnosis if diagnosed during follow-up) to the date of the earliest of COPD outcome (defined in the outcome measurement), death or the end of the study period (30 September 2021). Incidence rates for COPD were compared using two-sample Poisson tests. We defined three distinct regression models. In the first model, we adjusted for age and sex. Model 2 further adjusted for marital status, education level, smoking intensity, alcohol consumption, physical activity and BMI. Model 3 further adjusted for comorbidities and use of medications. Models 2 and 3 are the primary multivariable models in our analysis. One provides all potential confounding variables into the model (Model 3), and the other (Model 2) provides a simpler model (with less variables) which is less likely to be over-adjusted. In each of these models, we treated age as a continuous variable. We used Schoenfeld residuals to test for proportional hazard assumption ( P > 0.05).

We used smoking status, smoking intensity and cumulative dose to assess the impact of smoking on the association of tuberculosis with risk of COPD. Smoking status was categorized into current smokers if they smoked ≥1 cigarette per day for >1 year, former smokers if they had quit smoking for >1 year and never smokers for all others. Smoking intensity was divided into never smoking, <10, 10–20, ≥21 cigarettes per day. 30 , 31 Number of pack-years, representing cumulative dose, was calculated as (cigarettes per day/20) × smoking duration in years, and categorized into never smokers, <13, 13–24, ≥25 pack-years. 30 , 31 We combined former and current smokers when calculating smoking intensity and cumulative dose.

We also performed subgroup analyses to assess whether the associations between pulmonary tuberculosis and risk of COPD varied by age (35–49, 50–64 and ≥65 years), sex, smoking intensity, alcohol drinking, BMI (<24 or ≥24 kg/m 2 ), physical activity (<1 or ≥1 time/week) and education level. To evaluate whether an interaction was present, we used multivariable regression models with a multiplicative interaction term between each characteristic of interest and pulmonary tuberculosis. Then, we determined statistical significance for the interaction based on the maximum likelihood χ 2 from a nested model with and without the interaction term. 32

We calculated the population attributable fraction (PAF) of pulmonary TB and COPD using standard formulas 33 .

We conducted several sensitivity analyses. First, we excluded participants who started any COPD medications in the 1 year before the index date and those with any chest pain or dyspnoea/breathing difficulty diagnoses ( Supplementary Table S1 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online) as possible pre-symptoms of COPD. 34 Second, we further excluded incident COPD cases that occurred within the first year of follow-up or within 1 year of diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis and tuberculosis, to minimize reverse causation. Third, we used multiple imputation via chained equations (MICE) to impute missing values of covariates. Fourth, we altered the end of follow-up to 31 December 2019, in order to exclude the potential influence of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic on outdoor physical activity, hospital visits and air pollution 22 . Fifth, we also excluded participants with asthma, bronchiectasis or pneumonia at baseline. Finally, we calculated E-value to assess the potential effect of unmeasured confounders. 35

All statistical tests were two-sided; 95% confidence intervals were considered to assess statistical significance.
Results:
We recruited 477 046 residents who had registered in the CHERRY study during 1 January 2009 to 31 December 2014. We excluded 244 831 participants aged <35 years, 1552 participants with a previous history of COPD, 1008 participants with a previous history of cancer and 30 773 participants with missing values of covariates. Finally, we included a total of 198 882 participants in this study aged >35 years ( Figure 1 ). Median age of the study population was 46.5 [interquartile range (IQR), 40.5–56.2] ( Table 1 ); 51% of subjects were men.

Overall, a total of 1414 participants was identified with pulmonary tuberculosis, of whom 1413 were incident cases. The median follow-up time was 9.9 years (IQR, 8.8–11.1) and a total of 16 449 cases developed COPD during the study period ( Supplementary Table S4 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). Median follow-up times between enrolment and incident tuberculosis diagnosis, as well as tuberculosis and COPD diagnosis, were 3.1 (IQR, 0.8–6.2) and 3.1 (IQR, 0.9–6.2), respectively. In the full cohort, the cumulative incidence of COPD was 8.3%, among individuals with pulmonary tuberculosis this was 23.6% ( Figure 2 ). When using a secondary exposure classification of all tuberculosis, cumulative incidence of COPD was 16.5%. The association between pulmonary tuberculosis and COPD was present in all multivariable models. Hazards ratios, derived from multivariable models measuring the association between pulmonary tuberculosis and COPD, ranged from 2.63 (95% CI, 2.36–2.93) in Model 1 to 1.77 (1.59–1.97) in Model 3 ( Table 2 ). For the association between all tuberculosis and COPD, the HR ranged from 1.71 (1.51–1.94) in Model 1 (adjustment for age and sex) to 1.18 (1.04–1.34) in Model 3 (adjustment for all demographic and clinical variables). When using differing classifications of smoking ( Supplementary Table S5 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online) in model adjustments or a three-category variable for tuberculosis ( Supplementary Table S6 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online), results were similar. Using estimates of Model 2 and Model 3, the PAF for COPD due to pulmonary TB was 1.1% (0.9–1.3) and 0.5% (0.4–0.7), respectively.

When we further stratified our results to assess for interaction ( Figure 3 ), the relationship between pulmonary tuberculosis and increased risk of COPD was present across most but not all subgroups. An increased hazard of COPD was seen among persons aged 50–64 (aHR, 1.83; 1.56–2.15) and 65 years and above (aHR, 1.80; 1.50–2.16), but a weaker association was seen in those 35–49 years old (aHR, 1.40; 1.08–1.82). Associations between pulmonary tuberculosis and risk of COPD were observed among participants with poor education [less than high school: aHR, 1.90 (1.69–2.13); P interaction <0.001). We did not find evidence that smoking intensity, sex, alcohol use or physical activity were effect modifiers ( P interaction >0.05) ( Supplementary Tables S7 and S8 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online). When we restricted our analysis to all tuberculosis; only smoking intensity did not modify the association.

Sensitivity analyses did not meaningfully change our findings ( Table 3 ). When excluding participants who started any COPD medications in the 1 year before the index date and those with any chest pain or dyspnoea/breathing difficulty diagnoses, the aHRs were 1.91 (1.68–2.18) and 1.31 (1.13–1.52) for pulmonary tuberculosis and all tuberculosis exposure classifications, respectively. We also further excluded incident COPD cases occurring within the first year of follow-up, after which the corresponding aHRs were 1.69 (1.51–1.90) and 1.18 (1.04–1.35), respectively. When using MICE to impute missing values of covariates, the corresponding aHRs were 1.76 (1.59–1.95) and 1.15 (1.02–1.30), respectively. Upon restricting follow-up duration to 31 December 2019, the corresponding aHRs were 2.04 (1.79–2.33) and 1.27 (1.09–1.49), respectively. In further sensitivity analyses, we excluded participants with asthma, bronchiectasis or pneumonia at baseline, after which the corresponding aHRs were 1.86 (1.66–2.08) and 1.24 (1.09–1.41), respectively. E-values were 2.94 and 1.64 for the associations of pulmonary tuberculosis and all tuberculosis with risk of COPD, respectively.
Discussion:
In this large, population-based cohort study, we found that persons who developed tuberculosis were at severely elevated risk of subsequently developing COPD. This relationship between tuberculosis and subsequent COPD was present even after accounting for smoking intensity (i.e., smoking did not confound, modify or interact with the relationship) and remained after several sensitivity analyses and after adjusting for a large selection of potentially relevant lifestyle, demographic and clinical confounders. This finding supports and extends prior work demonstrating lung impairment after a tuberculosis episode, 6 , 36 , 37 showing subsequent severe clinical chronic lung disease as a result. This work provides empirical evidence that tuberculosis is an important and underrecognized risk factor for COPD. The relationship was larger when considering pulmonary tuberculosis rather than all tuberculosis, supporting the hypothesis that pulmonary activity and damage during disease may be one mechanism of subsequent elevated COPD risk. We further found that certain subgroups of participants (participants who were older and with lower education, BMI and physical activity) were at highest risk of developing COPD after tuberculosis, which may suggest that targeted follow-up after recovery from tuberculosis may be a pragmatic and meaningful intervention to prevent severe lung disease.

Although lung damage due to smoking is considered the primary cause of COPD, there has been a growing push to recognize other routes or groups of patients that do not smoke who are also at high-risk. 2 , 3 Alternative risk factors may represent contributions to future COPD cases and may provide more amenable intervention strategies. The World Health Organization currently does not recognize tuberculosis as a risk factor for COPD. Our findings suggest that tuberculosis patients have increased risk of COPD, after controlling for the smoking variable, and that a proportion of COPD is attributable to tuberculosis. The results highlight the push for tuberculosis to be included. 9 There is growing realization in the tuberculosis field that post-disease sequalae and morbidity are immense. 4 , 6 , 7 , 38 Recent estimates suggest that there are approximately 155 million survivors of tuberculosis globally 39 ; our results indicate this population must be prioritized or, at a minimum, followed to prevent further lung damage. 38 , 40

Importantly, we found subgroups of participants that were at highest risk of developing COPD after a tuberculosis episode, including persons with low education, low BMI and not as physically active. Prior studies have either not identified important subgroups of persons with prior tuberculosis that are at particularly high risk of COPD, or shown heterogeneous results. 9 , 41 Groups at high-risk of COPD in our study may be an overlapping population, representing populations with low socioeconomic status (i.e., persons with low socioeconomic status may have low BMI, education level, etc.), suggesting that post-tuberculosis lung damage leading to COPD may be concentrated in the most at-need populations. Pathways explaining how these secondary variables accentuate the relationship between tuberculosis and subsequent tuberculosis cannot be ascertained with our data; however we hypothesize that low BMI may represent a severe form or more advanced stage of tuberculosis. 42

Our study has several strengths, including the large sample size with a wealth of demographic and clinical information on included participants. Second, distinct from most other databases of this kind, important individual-level, lifestyle risk factor information was available, including extent of physical activity, smoking intensity and alcohol use, among others. Our results are subject to less recall biases, as participants were administered surveys at multiple time points and were followed over time through a comprehensive health insurance system that detected diagnoses rather than self-reported prior tuberculosis. The CHERRY study, like large health insurance system datasets in many European countries, covers almost the entire district population (>99% of area inhabitants), thereby minimizing chances of missed tuberculosis diagnosis. 19 Last, tuberculosis diagnoses were assessed and confirmed through ICD-10 coding rather than through retrospective diagnosis or recall through self-report, as seen in prior studies. 12–14 This allows for direct confirmation of tuberculosis diagnosis and reduces potential exposure misclassification.

There are limitations to our analysis. First, despite the strengths of the comprehensive health system that the CHERRY study provides, tuberculosis cases that are never diagnosed and subsequently resolve are not covered, leading to underdiagnosis of tuberculosis. 43 Second, we did not measure household socioeconomic status or smoke exposures (e.g., use of biomass fuels), potential confounders that may impact on both tuberculosis and COPD. Third, although we stratify our analysis by whether the tuberculosis episode was pulmonary, the type, severity and drug-resistance profile of tuberculosis was not recorded. Future studies should further refine specific features of tuberculosis that are more likely to lead to COPD. Fourth, residual or unmeasured confounding is possible. For example, we did not measure characteristics at the time of tuberculosis diagnosis. Despite this, the high observed E-values suggest that any unmeasured characteristics would need to be heavily influential to affect our findings. Last, an underlying lung damage or susceptibility prior to the development of both COPD and tuberculosis, not available within our cohort, may be the cause of both diseases.
Conclusion: In conclusion, in our study of almost 200 000 participants within a population-based cohort study of an entire district area in eastern China, we found a markedly higher risk of COPD among persons with a tuberculosis episode. Importantly, this relationship remained after accounting for participant smoking status and intensity and was more pronounced among people with pulmonary tuberculosis. These results suggest that a prior tuberculosis episode should be considered an important risk factor for COPD and that prevention of tuberculosis may have indirect, downstream individual- and population-level health benefits.
Ethics approval: The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Zhejiang University School of Public Health.
